title: Houthis, Red Sea And Oil: How The US-Iran War Opened A New Front Against Saudi Arabia
summary: A fragile truce in Yemen is rapidly unraveling as Iran-backed Houthi forces escalate missile, drone and maritime attacks that threaten Red Sea shipping and global energy markets. Renewed violence follows the US-Iran war and stalled peace talks over oil revenue and salary payments. Analysts warn the conflict could reignite full-scale war between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, with broader regional consequences for maritime security and oil routes.
content:
A fragile truce that had held in Yemen for more than four years is rapidly unravelling, with the Iran-backed Houthi militia and Saudi Arabia moving closer to another full-scale conflict.

The latest escalation follows the US war with Iran, which has reignited tensions between the two sides after years of relative calm. While Saudi Arabia has shown little appetite for another military confrontation, the Houthis appear determined to increase pressure on the kingdom to secure political and economic concessions inside Yemen, according to a New York Times ground report.

The conflict in Yemen had largely remained frozen since a truce was declared in 2022 after years of fighting between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis. The war had pushed Yemen to the brink of famine and left hundreds of thousands dead from violence, hunger and disease, stated the NYT report.

Although both sides had paused large-scale fighting, negotiations for a lasting peace gradually stalled. Saudi officials hoped the uneasy calm would continue, but the Houthis became increasingly frustrated over the lack of progress.

According to officials and diplomats familiar with the militia quoted by the NYT report, the Houthis believe they have much to gain from renewed confrontation, including access to Yemen’s oil revenue and greater political authority.

Researchers studying the group say the Houthis are acting not only in support of Iran but also to force Saudi Arabia and the international community to make concessions.

"The Houthis have one solution for every problem in the world, which is go to war," said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen-focused fellow at Chatham House.

Over the past week, the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia and targeted ships in the Red Sea, disrupting global energy markets. In response, the Saudi-led coalition has carried out airstrikes in Houthi-controlled territory for the first time in years.

"There is a real concern that the internal Yemeni war could reignite," said April Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute who previously worked on Yemen’s peace process at the United Nations.

The account is based on interviews with Yemeni officials, current and former Western diplomats involved in Yemen’s peace process and regional analysts, most of whom spoke anonymously because of the sensitivity of ongoing political negotiations.

The Houthis began as a small group of Shiite Muslim rebels in northern Yemen before capturing Sanaa in 2014 with Iranian support and overthrowing the internationally recognised government.

Saudi Arabia responded by leading a military coalition against the group, but the campaign became a lengthy and costly conflict. Under international pressure over Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, the kingdom later reduced its military involvement.

By 2022, the Houthis had established de facto control over northern Yemen, while the internationally recognised government retained nominal authority in the south with Saudi financial and military backing.

In late 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis came close to signing a preliminary peace agreement, described by officials as a "road map", with United Nations support. A major part of the proposal involved restoring salary payments to government employees in Houthi-controlled areas. Between $1 billion and $2 billion a year was expected to be funded largely through Yemeni oil revenue, according to Western diplomats and a Yemeni official.

However, the Hamas-led attack on Israel in October 2023 and Israel’s military campaign in Gaza derailed the peace process. The Houthis launched missiles and drones at Israel and ships in the Red Sea in support of Palestinians.

Saudi Arabia and international diplomats argued that those attacks violated the ceasefire underpinning the peace process, while the Houthis insisted their truce with Saudi Arabia remained intact.

During the Gaza war, the Houthis avoided attacking Saudi Arabia even as they intensified attacks in the Red Sea. After President Donald Trump began his second term in 2025, he designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation and launched a bombing campaign against them, worsening economic conditions in Houthi-controlled areas.

Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti accused Saudi Arabia of failing to implement the proposed peace agreement, particularly salary payments, and blamed the kingdom for restrictions on aviation and shipping to Yemen.

Saudi ambassador to Yemen Mohammed al-Jaber said Riyadh remained committed to de-escalation and a comprehensive peace, while accusing the Houthis of pursuing violence and serving foreign agendas.

After fighting resumed between the United States and Iran, analysts said the Houthis appeared to deepen their involvement. Following a dispute over an Iranian aircraft landing in Sanaa, the group declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Because of Yemen’s strategic position along the Red Sea, the Houthis are capable of disrupting global energy markets. Saudi Arabia, which normally exports most of its oil through the Strait of Hormuz, has been forced by the conflict to reroute shipments through the Red Sea.

On July 23, after the Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi oil tankers, Trump warned that the militia would face "major military punishment" if the attacks continued. He also said the Houthis had, "until now, acted very professionally and smart."
